# Το Καλοκαίρι Πριν τον Αποχαιρετισμό

Ο Αύγουστος είχε αρχίσει να μυρίζει φθινόπωρο.

Δεν ήταν κάτι που μπορούσες να δεις ή να ακούσεις — ήταν κάτι που *ένιωθες* στον αέρα, σαν μια υπόσχεση που δεν έχει δοθεί ακόμα αλλά είναι ήδη αναπόφευκτη. Ο Θανάσης το ένιωθε κάθε πρωί που ξυπνούσε και κοιτούσε το ταβάνι του δωματίου του, μετρώντας τις μέρες που απέμεναν σαν να μετρούσε τις σταγόνες μιας κλεψύδρας.

Είκοσι εννέα μέρες.

---

Βρίσκονταν στην παραλία, όπως κάθε βράδυ εκείνο το καλοκαίρι. Η Σοφία καθόταν ανάμεσα στα πόδια του, με την πλάτη ακουμπισμένη στο στήθος του, και κοιτούσαν τα κύματα να σβήνουν στην άμμο. Τα μαλλιά της μύριζαν αλατιλα και αντηλιακό και κάτι άλλο που ο Θανάσης δεν μπορούσε να ονομάσει αλλά ήξερε ότι θα το θυμόταν για πάντα.

«Πόσες ώρες είναι;» ρώτησε εκείνη ξαφνικά.

«Τι;»

«Αλεξανδρούπολη από Κρήτη. Πόσες ώρες.»

Ο Θανάσης δίστασε. Το είχε ψάξει ήδη — φυσικά το είχε ψάξει — αλλά δεν ήθελε να πει τον αριθμό δυνατά, σαν να τον έκανε πιο αληθινό.

«Πολλές,» είπε τελικά.

Η Σοφία γέλασε, ένα γέλιο μικρό και λυπημένο. «Πολλές. Ωραία απάντηση για μαθηματικό.»

«Μελλοντικό μαθηματικό.»

«Μελλοντικό νηπιαγωγό εγώ.» Έσφιξε τα χέρια του που ήταν τυλιγμένα γύρω της. «Θα με φωνάζεις "κυρία Σοφία";»

«Μόνο αν φέρεσαι άσχημα.»

Γέλασαν και οι δύο, και μετά σώπασαν, και η σιωπή ήταν βαριά με όλα όσα δεν έλεγαν.

---

Η αλήθεια ήταν αυτή: είχαν μιλήσει για όλα εκτός από το ένα πράγμα που μετρούσε. Είχαν μιλήσει για τα κοινόχρηστα, για τους συγκατοίκους, για τα μαθήματα. Η Σοφία είχε αγοράσει ήδη ένα μεγάλο μπλε βαλίτσα. Ο Θανάσης είχε κατεβάσει εφαρμογές για φθηνά εισιτήρια.

Αλλά κανείς δεν είχε πει: *Τι θα γίνουμε εμείς;*

Εκείνο το βράδυ, καθώς η θάλασσα σκούραινε και τα πρώτα αστέρια εμφανίζονταν ένα-ένα σαν να ντρέπονταν, η Σοφία μίλησε πρώτη.

«Φοβάμαι,» είπε απλά.

«Κι εγώ.»

«Όχι για τις σπουδές. Για μας.»

Ο Θανάσης έβαλε το πηγούνι του στον ώμο της. Μπορούσε να νιώσει την καρδιά της να χτυπά — ή ίσως ήταν η δική του, δεν ήξερε πια πού τελείωνε ο ένας και άρχιζε ο άλλος.

«Εγώ ξέρω ένα πράγμα,» είπε.

«Τι;»

«Ότι δεν υπάρχει κανένα μαθηματικό μοντέλο που να μετράει αυτό που νιώθω για σένα. Το έχω προσπαθήσει.»

Η Σοφία γύρισε να τον κοιτάξει. Στα μάτια της υπήρχε κάτι που έμοιαζε με κλάμα αλλά δεν ήταν — ήταν κάτι πιο δυνατό από κλάμα.

«Τα παιδιά στο νηπιαγωγείο λένε πάντα την αλήθεια,» είπε. «Γι' αυτό θέλω να δουλεύω μαζί τους. Γιατί δεν ξέρουν ακόμα να κρύβονται.»

«Τότε μίλα μου σαν παιδί.»

Σκέφτηκε για λίγο.

«Δεν θέλω να φύγεις.»

«Δεν θέλω να φύγεις κι εσύ.»

«Αλλά θα φύγουμε.»

«Θα φύγουμε.»

Το είπαν και οι δύο μαζί, σχεδόν ταυτόχρονα, και κάτι στον τρόπο που ακούστηκε — σαν ομολογία, σαν συμφωνία, σαν προσευχή — έκανε τον αέρα ελαφρύτερο.

---

Τις επόμενες μέρες δεν μίλησαν πολύ για το μέλλον. Αντίθετα, έζησαν το παρόν με μια ένταση που έκανε τα πάντα να φαίνονται πιο φωτεινά — τον καφέ το πρωί, τις βόλτες στην παλιά αγορά, τα βράδια με φίλους που κι αυτοί σκορπίζονταν σε διάφορες πόλεις.

Ο Θανάσης έμαθε ότι η Αλεξανδρούπολη έχει ωραίο λιμάνι. Η Σοφία έμαθε ότι η Κρήτη έχει τα καλύτερα χταπόδια στον κόσμο. Ανταλλάξανε αυτές τις πληροφορίες σαν δώρα.

Την τελευταία τους βραδιά, ξανά στην παραλία, ο Θανάσης έβγαλε από την τσέπη του ένα χαρτί διπλωμένο στα τέσσερα.

«Τι είναι αυτό;» ρώτησε η Σοφία.

«Ένας υπολογισμός.»

Το άνοιξε. Ήταν γεμάτο αριθμούς και βέλη και μικρές σημειώσεις στο περιθώριο.

«Αν ταξιδεύω μία φορά τον μήνα και εσύ μία φορά τον μήνα,» εξήγησε, «και αν εκμεταλλευόμαστε κάθε αργία και κάθε διακοπές, τότε θα είμαστε μαζί τουλάχιστον εξήντα τρεις μέρες τον χρόνο. Αυτό είναι περίπου το δεκαεπτά τοις εκατό του χρόνου.»

Η Σοφία τον κοίταξε.

«Δεκαεπτά τοις εκατό,» επανέλαβε.

«Ξέρω ότι ακούγεται λίγο—»

«Ακούγεται σαν εσένα.» Του χαμογέλασε. «Εσένα τον ηλίθιο που αγαπώ.»

Τον φίλησε πριν προλάβει να απαντήσει, και το χαρτί με τους υπολογισμούς πέταξε λίγο στον αέρα πριν προσγειωθεί στην άμμο, όπου έμεινε σαν μια μικρή, τετράγωνη υπόσχεση.

---

Έφυγαν με διαφορά τριών ημερών — πρώτα ο Θανάσης, μετά η Σοφία.

Στο λεωφορείο για το αεροδρόμιο, ο Θανάσης κοίταζε έξω από το παράθυρο και σκεφτόταν ότι η απόσταση είναι ένα παράξενο πράγμα. Μπορεί να μετρηθεί σε χιλιόμετρα, σε ώρες, σε εισιτήρια. Αλλά αυτό που ένιωθε για τη Σοφία δεν χωρούσε σε καμία μονάδα μέτρησης που γνώριζε.

Ίσως αυτό ήταν που τον έκανε να συνεχίσει τα μαθηματικά — η πεποίθηση ότι για κάθε πράγμα που δεν καταλαβαίνεις ακόμα, υπάρχει μια γλώσσα που δεν έχεις μάθει ακόμα.

Στην Αλεξανδρούπολη, η Σοφία έβαζε τα πράγματά της στο καινούριο της δωμάτιο και κολλούσε στον τοίχο μια φωτογραφία — οι δύο τους στην παραλία, με τη θάλασσα πίσω τους και τα μαλλιά τους ανακατεμένα από τον αέρα.

Κάτω από τη φωτογραφία, με μαρκαδόρο, έγραψε:

*17%*

Και χαμογέλασε.

results.llm_story:
# The Fork in the Road

The last exam paper had barely left Maria's hand before she collapsed dramatically onto the library steps, arms spread wide like she'd survived something biblical.

"We're done," she announced to the sky.

George sat beside her more quietly, turning his student ID over and over in his fingers. "We're done," he agreed, though it sounded different coming from him. More like a question.

They sat there for a while, watching other students pour out of the building behind them, some celebrating loudly, others wearing that same uncertain expression that George couldn't quite shake off. Four years of algorithms, data structures, programming languages, and theoretical frameworks had deposited them both here, on these concrete steps, with the uncomfortable freedom of *what now* stretching out ahead.

---

It had started three weeks earlier, during finals, when they'd both received the master's programme brochures in the mail. Their mother had stacked them neatly on the kitchen table, probably hoping they'd discuss them together over dinner like sensible adults.

Instead, Maria had grabbed hers while passing through, barely glancing at it, and George had spent forty-five minutes reading his cover to cover when he should have been studying distributed systems.

Maria had circled Digital Humanities with a red pen so immediately and so decisively that the pen had nearly gone through the page.

George had stared at the Quantum Computing brochure until the words blurred.

"You're not seriously considering that one," Maria had said, leaning over his shoulder while stealing grapes from the fruit bowl.

"Why not?"

"Because nobody knows what quantum computing *actually* is yet. You'd essentially be studying a very expensive mystery."

"That's exactly why," George said.

Maria had given him the look. The twin look, the one that meant *I understand you completely and I think you're being an idiot*, and walked away still eating his grapes.

---

Their conversations about it had been circling for weeks, never quite landing anywhere.

"I don't understand why you'd leave computer science behind," George said one evening, finding Maria surrounded by books that had no business being near a computer science student. Poetry collections. Historical manuscripts. A thick volume on medieval archiving systems.

"I'm not leaving it behind," she said, not looking up. "I'm pointing it at something more interesting."

"More interesting than the fundamental nature of computation itself?"

"George." She finally looked up. "We spent four years learning to build incredibly powerful tools. Don't you ever wonder what those tools are *for*? What they do to culture, to language, to the way humans remember things?" She held up the medieval archiving book. "There are thousands of manuscripts that nobody has properly analysed because there aren't enough human eyes or enough hours. We could change that. We could help historians find patterns that have been invisible for five hundred years."

George was quiet for a moment. "That's actually not terrible," he admitted.

"High praise from you." She threw a grape at him.

"But doesn't it feel like you'd be the computer science person in a room full of humanities people? Always translating?"

Maria smiled slowly. "Yes," she said. "Exactly that. I'd be the bridge. I like bridges."

George nodded, turning this over. He understood that. He just knew, with equal certainty, that he was not a bridge person.

He was a *what lies on the other side of the impossible* person.

---

Their father, a practical man who had spent thirty years as a civil engineer, listened to both of them explain their choices over Sunday dinner and then said nothing for a long moment.

"So one of you," he finally said, pointing his fork at Maria, "wants to use computers to understand the past." The fork swung to George. "And one of you wants to use physics to build computers that don't exist yet."

"That's a simplification," George started.

"It's a good simplification," Maria said.

Their father nodded slowly. "And you both studied the same thing for four years."

"Yes," they said together.

He looked at their mother. Their mother looked back at him. Some private parental communication passed between them that the twins had never been able to decode despite twenty-two years of observation.

"Good," their father said, and returned to his dinner.

"Good?" George pressed.

"It means we didn't raise the same person twice," their mother said simply. "That would have been a waste."

---

Back on the library steps, the afternoon was cooling down around them.

"Are you scared?" Maria asked.

George considered lying. "Quantum mechanics is genuinely terrifying," he said. "The more you understand it, the less sense it makes. I'll probably spend two years being confused at a very high level."

"I'll probably spend two years being the only person in every room who knows what an API is."

"You'll be insufferable."

"I'm already insufferable."

A group of their coursemates walked past, waving, shouting something about a celebration at a bar nearby. Maria waved back. George gave a small nod.

"Same starting point," Maria said quietly, watching them go.

"Very different directions," George agreed.

She nudged his shoulder with hers. It was a small gesture, the kind that had existed between them since they were old enough to sit up, a kind of morse code that meant something like *I see you* or *we're still us* or simply *okay*.

He nudged back.

They sat there a little longer, on the steps of the place that had made them both into something, before they would walk off separately toward the things they were still becoming.

The evening light made long shadows of them both, pointing in opposite directions across the pavement.

Neither of them mentioned it.

They didn't need to.

results.original_prompt: Write a short story: Two high school friends, Kostas and Eleni, are deciding on their university majors. One chooses to study Mechanical Engineering and the other chooses Nursing.
results.llm_story:
# The Fork in the Road

The souvlaki place on Ermou Street had been their spot since ninth grade. Same sticky table by the window, same argument about who got the last pita, same comfortable noise of the city pressing against the glass.

Kostas dropped his backpack on the chair across from Eleni and fell into his seat like something had knocked the air out of him.

"I sent it," he said.

Eleni looked up from her phone. "Sent what?"

"The application. Mechanical Engineering. Athens Polytechnic." He said it the way someone announces they've jumped off a cliff — after the fact, slightly amazed they did it.

Eleni set her phone face-down on the table. That was her tell. It meant she was actually paying attention.

"Your father must be thrilled," she said carefully.

"He doesn't know yet." Kostas picked up a napkin and folded it into a small, tight square. "He thinks I applied to Business Administration like my cousin Nikos."

"Kostas."

"I know."

She didn't push it. That was one of the things he appreciated most about Eleni — she understood when a subject had a door on it.

"What about you?" he asked. "You've been quiet all week. Quieter than usual, I mean. Which is saying something."

She smiled at that, just slightly. Outside, a tram rattled past and the window shuddered in its frame.

"I applied to Nursing," she said.

He waited for more. Nothing came.

"That's it? That's all I get?"

"What do you want me to say?"

"I don't know — something. You've been talking about medicine since we were fifteen. Your mother had that whole plan mapped out. Cardiology, she said. Private practice. The whole—"

"I know what my mother said." Eleni turned her coffee cup in small circles on the table. "I spent three weeks in the hospital last year with my grandmother. You remember."

"Of course."

"The doctors came in for maybe ten minutes a day. They were fine. They were professional." She paused. "But it was the nurses who actually *knew* her. They knew she was afraid of the dark, so they left the hallway light on. They knew she liked the news at seven o'clock. They knew when she was in pain before she even said anything." She looked up. "I want to be in the room, Kostas. Not just passing through it."

He was quiet for a moment. Outside, two pigeons argued over something on the pavement.

"Your mother is going to say it's a waste," he said. Not cruelly. Just honestly, the way old friends can be.

"She already did." Eleni picked her phone back up, then put it down again. "She used the word *waste* four times in one sentence. I counted."

"And?"

"And I told her that the woman who held her own mother's hand every night for two weeks was a nurse, and that didn't seem like a waste to me." She shrugged, but her eyes were bright. "She didn't have an answer for that."

Kostas laughed — a real one, surprised out of him. He leaned back in his chair and looked at his friend, this girl he'd known since they were fourteen and terrible at everything, and felt something he couldn't quite name. Pride, maybe. Or recognition.

"So," he said. "An engineer and a nurse."

"Assuming we both get in."

"We'll get in."

"You don't know that."

"I know we studied harder than anyone else in that school for three years." He held up his coffee cup. "We'll get in."

She picked hers up. The cups touched with a small, ceramic sound.

"Our parents are going to make our lives very difficult," she said.

"Probably."

"It's going to be hard."

"Definitely."

She nodded slowly, as if confirming something she'd already decided. "Good."

The souvlaki arrived. They split the last pita without arguing about it, which was new, and outside the city carried on in its loud and indifferent way, completely unaware that two people had just quietly chosen the shape of their lives.

# The Last Page

Maya had read *À la recherche du temps perdu* three times before she turned twenty.

Her professors called her gifted. Her classmates called her obsessed. Maya simply called it *necessary*.

She sat in the university library every evening, surrounded by worn copies of Flaubert, Baudelaire, and Camus, her fingers tracing sentences like they were old friends. While other students highlighted textbooks for exams, Maya read for something harder to name — a feeling, a truth, a conversation across centuries.

One rainy Thursday, a first-year student named Théo dropped into the chair across from her, desperate and pale.

*"I have to write about Madame Bovary by tomorrow,"* he whispered. *"I don't understand any of it."*

Maya looked up slowly. She closed her Proust.

*"Emma Bovary,"* she said quietly, *"is a woman who read too many romantic novels and believed life should feel like one."* She paused. *"She wasn't foolish. She was just hungry for something real in a world that offered her nothing."*

Théo stared at her. *"That's... actually beautiful."*

Maya smiled and slid her notebook across the table.

*"French literature doesn't give you answers,"* she said. *"It just makes you better at asking questions."*

Outside, the rain continued falling.

# The Number Whisperer

Maya was fifteen when her math teacher, Mr. Collins, ran out of things to teach her.

It wasn't arrogance that set her apart. It was the way she *saw* numbers — not as symbols on a page, but as living things with personalities and relationships.

One afternoon, Mr. Collins wrote a complex equation on the board that had stumped him for days.

"Can anyone solve this?" he asked, mostly to himself.

The classroom was silent.

Maya's pencil moved quietly. Thirty seconds later, she set it down.

Mr. Collins walked to her desk, studied her work, and slowly removed his glasses.

"Maya," he said quietly, "how did you do this?"

She shrugged. "The numbers were lonely on one side. I just moved them where they belonged."

He stared at her. "That's... not how mathematics works."

"Maybe," she smiled, "but it got the right answer."

Mr. Collins sent her work to a university professor that same evening. By Friday, Maya had a scholarship offer and an invitation to join a research team studying problems that had remained unsolved for decades.

She packed her backpack on Monday morning just like any other day.

To Maya, it was simple.

The numbers had just been waiting for someone to finally *listen*.

# The Perfect Team

Marcus slapped the buzzer before the host finished reading the number aloud.

"Fourteen thousand, four hundred and thirty-six," he said flatly, adjusting his glasses.

The host blinked at his answer card. "That is... correct."

Across the table, their opponents exchanged a nervous glance. The crowd murmured. Priya just smiled into her water glass, completely unsurprised. She had watched Marcus do this since seventh grade, back when he used to multiply license plate numbers for fun during long car rides.

The math rounds dissolved quickly after that. Marcus was somewhere else entirely during those minutes, his eyes slightly unfocused, his fingers tapping a quiet rhythm only he could hear. Priya would lean back in her chair and let him work.

Then the categories shifted.

*Poetry and Language. Identify the author and the work.*

The host read a single line. *"I am large, I contain multitudes."*

Priya's hand was already moving. "Walt Whitman. *Song of Myself.*"

"Correct."

Marcus exhaled slowly. Poetry made him feel like he was trying to catch smoke. The words slid around, refused to stay numerical, refused to behave. He watched Priya answer four more in a row, her voice calm and certain, like someone reading from a page only she could see.

During the break, they stood by the vending machines in the hallway.

"How do you just *know* those?" Marcus asked, genuinely baffled.

Priya considered the question seriously. "I don't know. The lines just sound like themselves. Like they couldn't have been written any other way." She paused. "How do you calculate that fast?"

Marcus shrugged. "The numbers just fall into place."

She nodded slowly. They stood there a moment, two people who had spent years being slightly mysterious to each other, and found that comfortable.

They won the competition by eleven points.

On the drive home, Marcus multiplied the winning margin by every number he could think of, and Priya quietly recited Whitman to the passing streetlights, and neither of them felt the need to explain themselves at all.

— Καλημέρα σε όλους. Έχουμε πολλά να συζητήσουμε σήμερα.

Ο **Υπουργός Οικονομικών Νίκος Σταύρου** κοίταξε τα νούμερα στο laptop του και 溜έβγαλε ένα βαθύ αναστεναγμό.

— Τα έσοδα δεν πάνε καλά, κυρία Πρωθυπουργέ.

— Δεν πάνε *ακόμα* καλά, τον διόρθωσε η **Υπουργός Ανάπτυξης Μαρία Κωστοπούλου** με ένα χαμόγελο. — Το νέο πρόγραμμα για τις μικρές επιχειρήσεις χρειάζεται χρόνο.

Ο **Υπουργός Παιδείας Θανάσης Λέκκας** σήκωσε το χέρι του.

— Μιλώντας για χρόνο... τα σχολεία χρειάζονται επειγόντως νέα βιβλία.

— Και νέα κτίρια, πρόσθεσε ήσυχα η **Υπουργός Υγείας Σοφία Αντωνίου**, χωρίς να σηκώσει τα μάτια από τις σημειώσεις της.

Ακολούθησε μια ζωηρή συζήτηση. Φωνές ανέβηκαν, κατέβηκαν, κάποιος ανέτρεψε τον καφέ του — ήταν ο Νίκος, φυσικά — και η γραμματέας **Κατερίνα** έτρεξε με χαρτοπετσέτες.

Στο τέλος, μετά από δύο ώρες, η Ελένη χτύπησε ελαφρά το τραπέζι.

— Συμφωνούμε λοιπόν. Προτεραιότητα στην παιδεία, στήριξη στις επιχειρήσεις, και ο Νίκος βρίσκει τα χρήματα.

Ο Νίκος άνοιξε το στόμα του.

— Μα...

— Εξαιρετικά, είπε η Ελένη και έκλεισε τον φάκελό της. — Ίδια ώρα την επόμενη εβδομάδα.

Καθώς έφευγαν, η Μαρία χαμογέλασε στον Θανάση.

— Πάντα έτσι τελειώνει.

— Ναι, είπε εκείνος. — Αλλά κάπως τα καταφέρνουμε.

*Και είχε δίκιο.*

results.title: Cooking Skills
results.original_prompt: Write a short story about a couple where one partner is a good cook and the other doesn’t even know how to boil an egg
results.llm_story:
# The Learning Curve

Maya could make a roux without looking at the pan.

She could tell by smell alone when garlic was about to burn, could taste a sauce and know instinctively that it needed thirty seconds more acid and a pinch of something smoky. Her hands moved around the kitchen the way other people's hands moved across piano keys — without thinking, with absolute confidence.

Daniel could not boil an egg.

This was not an exaggeration. Three weeks into their relationship, Maya had come home to find him standing over the stove looking genuinely betrayed, staring at something grey and rubbery floating in water that had gone cold.

"I thought it would just... happen," he said.

She had loved him anyway.

---

Four years later, they had an arrangement. Maya cooked. Daniel did everything else — the shopping, the washing up, the setting of the table with a care that bordered on ceremony. He lit candles on Tuesday nights for no reason. He always bought the good olive oil even though he couldn't taste the difference, because she could.

It worked beautifully, mostly.

The problem arrived on a Thursday in November, when Maya slipped on the front step and fractured her wrist. Nothing dramatic. Just a quiet crack and then a cast from her palm to her elbow, white and inconvenient and deeply, deeply annoying.

"I'll cook," Daniel said immediately.

Maya looked at him with the careful expression of someone who loved a person very much and was choosing her words accordingly.

"You don't have to—"

"I want to."

---

The first night he made pasta. He called his mother twice, his college roommate once, and watched four separate YouTube videos about salting water. He set off the smoke alarm twice despite the fact that boiling water produces no smoke, a mystery neither of them could explain.

The pasta was slightly too soft. The sauce came from a jar, which he'd warmed in a pan and added things to — butter, a little of the pasta water, some basil he'd torn up hopefully.

Maya ate every bite.

"It's good," she said, and meant it enough that it counted.

"You're being kind."

"I'm being accurate. The basil was a good call."

He looked so unreasonably pleased that she had to look away.

---

He got slightly better every day. Not good — not even close to good — but *better*, which felt like its own kind of miracle. He learned that heat was a dial, not a switch. He learned that tasting as you go was not optional. He burned things and under-seasoned things and once produced a soup that Maya described, diplomatically, as "interesting."

But he kept going. He left handwritten notes on the counter — *garlic goes in AFTER onion is soft* — like a student studying for an exam that mattered.

One evening she sat on the kitchen stool, cast propped on the counter, watching him concentrate over a pan of chicken thighs with the same focused expression he used for spreadsheets and crossword puzzles. His tongue was pressed between his teeth. He was listening to the sizzle the way she'd once told him to, trying to hear what it meant.

"You're not bad at this," she said.

"I'm terrible at this."

"You're not *bad* at it."

He looked up, and she realised she'd said something that landed differently than she'd intended — something truer and more tender than a cooking lesson deserved.

"I just didn't have a reason to learn before," he said simply, and turned back to the pan.

---

The cast came off six weeks later. Maya stood in the kitchen that first evening, rolling her wrist experimentally, feeling the strange lightness of it.

Daniel was already at the stove.

"I thought I'd cook," he said. "If that's okay."

The chicken was a little dry. The vegetables were slightly overdone. He'd forgotten to season the water again.

Maya sat at the table he'd set with candles — a Tuesday habit that had quietly spread to every night — and ate everything on her plate.

"Next time," she said, "I'll show you the roux."

He smiled like she'd offered him something valuable.

She had.

# The Coin Toss

The hallway outside the principal's office smelled like old coffee and anxiety.

Eleni leaned against the wall, arms crossed, watching Iasonas smooth the front of his floral skirt — the yellow one with the small white daisies that he'd worn at least three times that week already.

"We should both go in," Eleni said.

"The note said one representative." Iasonas didn't look up. He was focused on a loose thread near the hem, deciding whether to pull it.

"The note said *a* representative. That's different."

"It really isn't."

They had been friends since the fourth grade, which meant they had also been arguing since the fourth grade. The incident that morning — a chair thrown, a window cracked, two boys sent home before lunch — had left the classroom feeling hollow and strange, and neither of them particularly wanted to walk through that door and explain what they had or hadn't seen.

"You go," Iasonas said finally. "You're better at talking to adults."

"You're better at *not* saying things you'll regret."

He laughed at that, short and genuine. "That's a terrible reason."

"It's an accurate reason."

He left the thread alone and looked at her properly. "I'll go. I was sitting closer to where it happened. I actually saw it."

Eleni considered this. It was true. She had been at the board, writing something she couldn't even remember now, when the sound had split the room open.

"They might give you a hard time," she said quietly. Not about what he'd seen. They both understood what she meant.

Iasonas shrugged, and it was the kind of shrug that had years of practice behind it — not careless, but *settled*. "Principal Markos has never said anything to me."

"There's always a first time."

"Then I'll handle a first time." He straightened up, ran a hand through his hair, and knocked twice on the frosted glass door before Eleni could say anything else.

She watched his outline through the glass as the door opened and he stepped inside.

She sat down on the wooden bench to wait, the hallway quiet except for the distant sound of a classroom reciting something in unison — history, maybe, or geography — the ordinary rhythm of the school continuing around the broken place the morning had left behind.

After twelve minutes, the door opened again.

Iasonas came out, closed it carefully behind him, and sat beside her.

"Well?" she asked.

"He wanted to know if anyone had provoked it. I told him what I saw." He paused. "He listened."

"That's it?"

"He also said my skirt was very cheerful." Iasonas looked at her sideways. "I think he meant it as a compliment."

Eleni thought about this. "That's either very good or very strange."

"Probably both," Iasonas said.

# The Starting Point

Principal Hartmann rewound the footage three times.

Two girls. Locker room. Seven minutes. One phone missing.

*I have to start from somewhere*, he thought, and reached for his phone to call Sofia's classroom first.

She arrived at his office with her hands in her jacket pockets, short hair slightly disheveled, meeting his eyes without flinching. He'd dealt with Sofia before. Tardiness, mostly. Once, an argument with a PE teacher about the uniform policy.

"You know why you're here?" he asked.

"The phone," she said. "I heard."

He asked his questions carefully. Her answers were consistent, calm, and specific. She'd been at her locker, she said. Left before Maria. She even remembered the combination she'd been struggling with.

He thanked her and called Maria next.

Maria sat down quietly, folded her hands, and smiled in that barely-visible way she had. She answered everything softly and without hesitation.

It was only when Hartmann asked a second time about the sequence of events that something small shifted. A pause. A recalibration.

He checked the timestamp again. The camera angle was poor, but the *duration* each girl spent near the far lockers was right there in the footage.

Sofia: forty seconds.

Maria: four minutes, twelve seconds.

He found the phone in Maria's bag twenty minutes later. She cried immediately, which told him she'd been carrying the weight of it all morning.

Hartmann sat back after she left with the counselor.

He had almost started from the wrong place. He'd looked at Sofia's jacket, her hair, her history of *being noticed*, and called her first — as if visibility were the same thing as guilt, as if the girl who drew no attention to herself couldn't possibly be worth a second look.

*That's the thing about starting points*, he thought, straightening the papers on his desk. *They reveal less about the case than they do about you.*

He made a note to review the school's locker policy. Then he made another note, more private, in the margin.

*Be more careful.*

# The 6:47 Train

Marcus heard the front door close at 6:12 every morning. He knew the exact time because he had started listening for it.

From his bedroom he could hear his father moving through the kitchen before dawn - the coffee maker, the quiet shuffle of dress shoes on tile, the particular sound the coat closet made when it opened. Then the door, and then silence.

By the time Marcus came downstairs, his mother was already at the counter.

"Peanut butter or turkey?" she asked without turning around.

"Turkey." He climbed onto the barstool and watched her work. She moved efficiently, the way people move when they have done something so many times that their hands no longer need instructions.

His little sister Penny appeared in her socks, sliding the last three feet into the kitchen.

"Peanut butter," Penny announced.

"I know," their mother said.

---

Their father's name was David, and he was trying to make partner.

This was a fact that existed in the house the way weather exists - not chosen, not permanent, but real and worth accounting for. It had been true for two years. It would be true, they understood, for a little while longer.

He called at 6:30 most evenings, during the commute home.

"How was school?" he asked Marcus one Tuesday, his voice slightly compressed through the phone speaker.

"We did fractions."

"Are they making sense?"

"Not really."

"I'll look at them with you tonight."

He got home at 8:14. Marcus was still at the kitchen table, which his mother had quietly arranged. She brought David a plate of food and sat with them while he worked through the worksheet with Marcus, still in his work clothes, his tie loosened.

"See, you already understand it," David said. "You just don't trust yourself yet."

Marcus looked at the paper. He thought maybe his father was right.

---

On a Wednesday in October, their mother sat at the same table after both kids were in bed, with a cup of tea and a permission slip she needed to sign and a permission slip she needed to find, and a mental list of things she was behind on, and a separate mental list of things she was worried about, and she sat there for a while just breathing.

When David came in she didn't move.

He set down his bag and looked at her and said, "Tell me."

"I'm just tired," she said. "It's fine. It's not a complaint."

"I know it's not a complaint." He sat down across from her. "Tell me anyway."

So she did. She told him about Penny's trouble with her reading group, and the parent-teacher conference she had rescheduled twice, and the way Marcus had seemed quieter lately, and the thing she couldn't name exactly - the feeling of being the person who holds all the small pieces while also missing another person.

He listened. He didn't offer solutions, which was the right choice.

"I'm going to talk to them," he said. "About the hours. I don't know what they'll say."

"You don't have to do that."

"I want to." He picked up the permission slip. "What's this for?"

"Field trip. Natural history museum."

"Can I chaperone?"

She looked at him. "You'd have to take a day."

"I know." He found a pen in his jacket pocket. "Sign it. Put me down as a chaperone."

---

The field trip was on a Friday. David wore jeans, which Marcus found slightly embarrassing and then, after a few minutes, didn't mind at all.

At the dinosaur exhibit, Penny held his hand and asked questions he couldn't fully answer, and he said *I don't know, let's find out* enough times that she started saying it too.

On the bus home, Marcus sat next to him.

"Dad?"

"Yeah."

"Are you going to make partner?"

David thought about it honestly. "I don't know. Maybe."

"What happens if you don't?"

"Then I don't." He looked out the window. "That wouldn't be the worst thing."

Marcus considered this. Outside, the city moved past in its ordinary way.

"Mom packs really good lunches," Marcus said, for no clear reason.

David smiled. "I know she does."

"She puts a note in sometimes. A little drawing."

"Does she?"

"A dinosaur today, actually." Marcus paused. "I saved it."

David nodded slowly, looking at his son, thinking about his wife at the counter in the early morning, thinking about all the things that hold a family together - the visible things and the invisible ones, the ones that show up on a balance sheet and the ones that never could.

"That sounds like her," he said.

The bus pulled toward home.

Maya signed without reading it. She'd read it a hundred times before, at this same clinic, for this same child, who seemed to collect ear infections the way other toddlers collected stickers.

"How's the paperwork business?" Daniel murmured.

"Booming," she said. "How's the rocking business?"

"Steady demand."

Theo stirred, turned his face toward Maya, and made a sound that wasn't quite a word. She took him from Daniel's arms and the handoff was seamless, the way it always was — a transfer of weight they'd both learned to carry.

Daniel stretched his back quietly and sat down in one of the plastic chairs. Maya kept moving.

Left, right. Left, right.

# The Extra Hour

The first time Giorgos came home after midnight, Elena had fallen asleep on the couch with the television still on. He kissed her forehead and she stirred just enough to mumble something about dinner being in the oven.

It was dry. He ate it anyway and felt terrible about that.

---

By the third week, she had stopped leaving dinner out.

She didn't say anything about it. That was the part that unsettled him most — Elena, who had an opinion about everything, who argued passionately about which side of the bed was warmer and why the neighbor's cat was *deliberately* antagonizing her, had gone quiet. She moved around the apartment like someone being careful not to break something.

"Work is brutal right now," he told her on a Tuesday, not quite meeting her eyes. "The Papadimitriou account. You know how it is."

"I know," she said.

She didn't ask follow-up questions anymore. She used to ask too many. He had once found that exhausting.

---

Her name was Sofia. She worked in the building two floors above his office and she laughed at everything he said, which he had initially found charming and was beginning to find slightly hollow. She made him feel interesting. He was starting to understand that feeling interesting and *being* interesting were not the same thing, and that he had perhaps confused the two for several months.

He thought about this on the metro home, watching his own reflection in the dark window.

---

Elena was awake when he got in. She was sitting at the kitchen table with a cup of tea that had clearly gone cold, and she was looking at him in a way that made his chest feel like it was full of wet concrete.

"I found a receipt," she said simply. "A restaurant. Last Thursday. You told me you were in a meeting until ten."

He opened his mouth.

She raised one hand, very slightly. *Don't.*

"I've known for a while," she said. "I think I've known longer than I wanted to admit." She wrapped both hands around the cold mug. "I kept waiting for you to come back. The real you. The one I married." She paused. "I don't think he's coming."

"Elena—"

"I'm not angry," she said, and the terrifying thing was that she meant it. Anger would have been easier. Anger would have meant there was still heat between them. "I'm just very, very tired, Giorgos."

He sat down across from her. The kitchen felt enormous.

"I'm sorry," he said. The words were true and they were also completely insufficient and he knew it.

She nodded slowly, as if he had confirmed something she had already made peace with.

"You should sleep in the guest room tonight," she said. "We can talk tomorrow. Properly." She finally stood, poured the cold tea down the sink, and rinsed the mug with the careful, deliberate movements of someone holding themselves together through routine.

At the doorway she stopped, her back still to him.

"I really loved you," she said. Not *love.* The past tense landed in the room like something heavy being set down for the last time.

Then she walked down the hall, and her bedroom door closed quietly.

Not a slam. That was the worst part.

A slam would have meant she still cared enough to be furious. The quiet click of that door was the sound of someone who had already done their grieving — alone, in the dark, while he was somewhere else entirely, making someone else laugh.

Giorgos sat at the kitchen table for a long time.

Outside, Athens hummed and glittered, indifferent and alive.

# Last Call

The ring was still new on Maria's finger when George spread the lease across the kitchen table like a treasure map.

"Look at this place," he said, tapping the photograph. "Corner location. High foot traffic. We build something *ours*."

Maria traced the edges of the photo with her fingernail. She was already smiling before she agreed.

---

They named it **Copper & Rye** and painted the door themselves on a Sunday in October, arguing cheerfully about whether burgundy was too dark. George won. Maria was right. They were happy.

The first months were electric. They worked side by side behind the bar, learning the rhythms of strangers — who needed a quiet pour and who needed conversation, who was celebrating and who was quietly drowning. They fell into bed each night exhausted and satisfied, smelling of citrus and whiskey.

Business grew. That was the problem, eventually. Business grew.

---

They hired staff. A bartender named Derek who knew every classic cocktail and told stories that made the whole room lean in. Two servers. A weekend DJ who brought crowds that spilled onto the sidewalk.

The success meant longer hours, and longer hours meant they stopped working the same shifts.

George closed on Fridays and Saturdays. Maria opened Tuesday through Thursday. They began leaving each other notes on the refrigerator instead of having conversations.

*Your dinner is wrapped in foil.*

*Don't forget the liquor order.*

*I'll be home late.*

The notes got shorter. Then they stopped altogether because there didn't seem to be much left to say in that format.

---

Her name was Claire. She came in every Friday, always sat at the far end of the bar, always ordered the same Negroni. George told himself he was just being attentive. Good hospitality. He told himself that for about three weeks.

He told himself a lot of things in those months. That he and Maria had simply grown into a business partnership. That the distance between them was practical, logistical, nobody's fault. That what happened with Claire on a rainy November night, after last call, after the staff had gone home and the chairs were up on the tables — that it was a mistake born of loneliness rather than a choice born of character.

He was wrong about that last part.

---

Maria found out the way people usually do. Not dramatically. Not with a confrontation in the rain. She found a message on his phone while he was in the shower, read it in about four seconds, and sat down on the edge of the bed very quietly.

When George came out, she was still sitting there.

She didn't cry. That surprised him, and it surprised her too. She just looked at him with an expression he had never seen on her face before — not anger exactly, but something more final than anger. Recognition, maybe. Like something she had half-suspected had simply been confirmed.

"I think you should stay at Derek's tonight," she said.

He started to speak.

"George." Her voice was steady. "Please just go."

---

The lawyers were civil. They sold Copper & Rye eight months later to a couple from out of town who immediately repainted the door — a pale gray that Maria privately thought was worse than her original suggestion.

She drove past it once, about a year later, on an idle afternoon. The sign was different. The windows had new trim. It looked like a completely different place, which she supposed it was.

She didn't stop.

She drove home, made herself tea, and sat by the window for a while, thinking about the Sunday they'd painted that door together. How they'd laughed. How certain everything had felt.

How certain everything had felt.

She finished her tea and washed the cup and got on with the rest of her life, which turned out, in time, to be a good one.

But she never wore the ring again, and she never ordered a Negroni, and she never quite trusted the particular happiness that arrives all at once, bright and complete, asking nothing yet.

results.llm_story:
# The Weight of the Gavel

Judge Eleanor Vasquez had seen hundreds of custody cases in her twelve years on the family court bench. She told herself that familiarity made her better at the job. On difficult mornings, she almost believed it.

She opened the Papadopoulos file on a Tuesday.

---

Nikos and Maria had been married for nine years. By all accounts, the first five had been good ones. There were photographs in the file — submitted as evidence of a stable home environment — that showed a family that looked genuinely happy. Birthday parties with blue and white balloons. A camping trip somewhere with pine trees. Two small faces, a boy named Theo, age seven, and a girl named Sofia, age five, grinning at the camera with the complete confidence of children who had never considered that their world might change.

The last four years had been something else.

The attorneys had submitted their briefs. A guardian ad litem had spent six weeks interviewing teachers, neighbors, and the children themselves. A child psychologist had filed a forty-page report. Judge Vasquez had read everything twice.

Nikos was a contractor who worked long hours but had never missed a school play or a pediatrician appointment when he could help it. His sister lived nearby and helped with the children regularly. He had a temper — two neighbors mentioned it, and Maria's attorney had made considerable use of that fact — but there was no evidence it had ever been directed at Theo or Sofia. His apartment, established after the separation, was modest but had a bedroom for each child, decorated with things he had clearly chosen carefully. Theo's had a poster of a soccer player. Sofia's had a shelf of books at exactly the right height for a five-year-old.

Maria was a nurse who worked rotating shifts, which complicated scheduling but also demonstrated, her attorney argued, a woman of discipline and responsibility. She had been the primary caregiver during the marriage, handling most of the school pickups, the sick days, the homework. She was quieter than Nikos, more organized. The psychologist noted that both children, when asked to draw their family, drew themselves standing next to their mother.

There was no villain in the file. That was what made it hard.

Judge Vasquez had learned early in her career that the worst custody cases were not the ones with a clear bad actor. Those were painful but navigable. The worst cases were the ones where two decent, wounded people both genuinely loved their children and both genuinely believed — with some justification — that they were the better choice.

She read the guardian ad litem's summary one more time.

*Theo has expressed a preference to live primarily with his father but becomes visibly distressed when asked to elaborate, suggesting awareness of loyalty conflict. Sofia has not expressed a clear preference but shows elevated anxiety responses in structured interview settings. Both children demonstrate secure attachment to both parents. Both children would benefit from maximum contact with both parents. The disruption of the current arrangement carries risk. The continuation of the current arrangement also carries risk.*

Judge Vasquez set the file down and looked out her window at the parking lot below. A woman was helping a small child out of a car seat. She watched until they disappeared through a door.

---

In the courtroom, Nikos sat on one side and Maria on the other. They did not look at each other. They had the careful, exhausted stillness of people who had been fighting for so long that they had forgotten what resting felt like.

Judge Vasquez read her decision into the record.

Primary physical custody would be awarded to Maria. The reasoning was methodical and documented: Maria's historical role as primary caregiver, the consistency of routine she could provide, the psychologist's findings regarding the children's attachment patterns, the proximity of Maria's home to the school the children currently attended.

Nikos would have the children every other weekend, alternating holidays, and two evenings per week. The order strongly encouraged both parents to pursue co-parenting counseling. It noted, in language that was formal but not unkind, that the court expected both parents to speak of the other with respect in the presence of the children.

Maria closed her eyes briefly when she heard the decision. It was not triumph. It looked more like relief mixed with something heavier — the understanding, perhaps, that winning in family court still meant your family was broken.

Nikos stared at the table in front of him. His jaw was tight. His attorney placed a hand briefly on his arm.

After the courtroom cleared, Judge Vasquez sat alone for a moment before her next case was called.

She thought about Theo's soccer poster. She thought about Sofia's bookshelf.

She thought about the photograph from the camping trip — the pine trees, the four of them together, everyone squinting happily into the sun — and she wondered, as she always did, whether she had gotten it right.

She never fully knew. That was the part of the job that no amount of experience had made easier.

She picked up the next file.

results.llm_story:
# The Weight of Love

Karen drove the same route every morning, past the gas station with the broken sign and the church with the good parking lot, until she reached the pale yellow house on Sycamore Street where their mother had lived for thirty-one years.

She let herself in with her key.

"Mom? It's me."

Eleanor was already awake, sitting in the recliner with the television on too loud, the way she always had it now. She was smaller than she used to be. Karen noticed this every single day and it never stopped surprising her.

"You don't have to come every morning," Eleanor said, which was also something she said every day.

"I know." Karen set her bag on the counter and started opening cabinets. "Oatmeal or eggs?"

"Surprise me."

She made eggs.

---

Her brother David called while the butter was melting in the pan. His name lit up the screen and she let it ring twice before answering, tucking the phone between her ear and shoulder.

"Hey," he said. He was in Seattle. He was always in Seattle. "How is she?"

"The same. Maybe a little more tired than yesterday."

"Did you talk to the doctor about adjusting the—"

"Yes, David. I talked to the doctor."

A pause. She could hear his office in the background. The quiet, climate-controlled hum of his important life.

"I called the billing department at St. Michael's," he said. "That last invoice was wrong. I got them to reprocess it. And I set up the automatic payment for the home health aide, in case you ever need—"

"She doesn't want a home health aide."

"I know, but in case."

Karen watched the eggs and didn't say anything.

"I'm just trying to help," David said.

"I know you are."

She meant it. She did. But there was a particular loneliness in being the one who was *here*, and she hadn't yet found the words for it that wouldn't sound like an accusation. She didn't want to fight. She was too tired to fight.

"She asked about you yesterday," Karen said, softening. "She wanted to know if you were eating enough."

David laughed, and for a moment he sounded like her brother again, the one who used to steal the good cereal and blame it on the dog. "That sounds right."

"She's still your mother from a thousand miles away."

"I know." His voice shifted into something quieter. "I know she is."

---

After breakfast, Karen sorted the medications into the weekly pill organizer that she'd bought to replace the one their mother kept mixing up. She set a glass of water on the side table. She washed the pan and wiped down the stove.

Eleanor watched her from the recliner.

"You look tired, sweetheart."

"I'm fine, Mom."

"You've been fine for two years." Eleanor reached out and caught Karen's wrist as she passed. Her grip was lighter than it used to be, but it still meant something. "I see you, you know. I see what you do."

Karen sat on the edge of the couch. She hadn't planned to sit down. She had three things to do before work.

"David worries too," Eleanor said. "He just worries in the way he knows how. He always needed to fix things. Even when he was small." She smiled at something Karen couldn't see. "You were the one who would just sit with me when I was sad. You didn't try to fix it. You just stayed."

Karen looked at her hands.

"I'm not keeping score," Eleanor said. "I hope you two aren't either."

---

That night, Karen texted David a photo of their mother asleep in the recliner with the television still on, a soft blue light across her face, looking peaceful.

*She had a good day*, Karen wrote.

David replied quickly. *Thank you for being there. I mean it. I really mean it.*

Karen set the phone down and looked out her kitchen window at the dark street. She thought about calling him back. She thought about saying all the things that had been collecting in her chest like stones — the exhaustion, the loneliness, the grief of watching someone disappear slowly, the strange resentment she felt and then felt guilty for feeling.

Instead she typed: *I know you do.*

And then, because it was also true: *She loves you so much.*

Three dots appeared. Disappeared. Appeared again.

*I'm going to come visit. Next month. I'll book it tonight.*

Karen smiled at her phone in the dark kitchen.

*She'll make me cook for all of us*, she wrote back.

*Good*, David said. *You need a break.*

She turned off the light and went to bed, and for the first time in a while, she didn't feel quite so alone in it.

The phone call came on a Tuesday morning, just as Nikos was pouring his first coffee and Maria was rushing to find her car keys.

"Your mother fell on the back steps," their father Stavros said, his voice unusually small. "They are putting a cast on her leg now. The doctor says six weeks, maybe more."

Nikos and Maria arrived at the hospital within minutes of each other. Their mother, Eleni, sat propped up in the hospital bed looking more embarrassed than hurt, waving her hand dismissively at the nurses as if the whole situation were a minor inconvenience she had personally caused out of stubbornness.

"It was that broken step," she said firmly. "I told your father about that step for two years."

Stavros stood in the corner saying nothing, which was probably wise.

On the drive home, Nikos and Maria walked slightly ahead of their parents and spoke in low, careful voices.

"I can't stay," Maria said immediately. "I have the Thessaloniki project. My boss has already been patient with me and I cannot ask him again."

"I have a job too," Nikos said.

"You can work from home. You always say you prefer it."

"That is completely different from actually doing it."

"Nikos."

He looked at her. She had dark circles under her eyes that he hadn't noticed before. He knew she had been struggling at work for months, quietly, without telling anyone. That was Maria's way.

"Fine," he said, and she grabbed his arm with both hands.

"I will come every weekend," she promised. "Every single one."

---

The first week was harder than Nikos had imagined. Not because of the cooking, which he actually found he didn't mind. He made simple things at first — lentil soup, baked chicken, the rice dish his mother had taught him years ago that he had never made for himself. His father ate everything without complaint, which was itself a kind of miracle.

The harder part was the house. It breathed differently when you were inside it all day. He heard things he had never noticed — the particular way the refrigerator hummed, the pigeons on the roof, his mother calling his name from the bedroom every hour or so for things she could have waited to ask together but didn't, because she was bored and in pain and felt guilty about being both.

"Nikos, can you bring me my blue cardigan?"

"Nikos, did you add salt to the soup?"

"Nikos, call your sister and tell her to bring those biscuits I like when she comes."

"Mama, I am right here. You can tell me and I will tell her."

"I want to tell her myself. But also tell her."

He brought her cardigan. He added salt. He called Maria.

By the third week, something shifted. He stopped fighting the slowness of the days and started moving inside them differently. He fixed the broken step — finally — on a quiet Wednesday afternoon, and felt unreasonably satisfied about it. He learned that his father liked his coffee slightly cooler than his mother always made it, something Stavros had apparently never mentioned in forty years of marriage. He sat with his mother in the evenings and she told him stories about her own mother, stories he had never heard, and he wished he had brought something to write them down with.

Maria came every weekend, as promised. She brought the biscuits. She took over the cooking on Saturdays so Nikos could drive to the city and see his friends, and when he came back on Sunday evenings the house smelled like her cooking, which was better than his, and he told her so.

"Don't tell Mama that," she said.

"She already knows."

They sat on the back steps together — the fixed ones — drinking wine after their parents had gone to sleep, and Maria said, "Is it terrible? Really?"

Nikos thought about it honestly.

"No," he said. "It is strange. But no."

She leaned her head on his shoulder briefly, the way she used to do when they were children.

"I'll stay the whole of next weekend," she said. "You can go Friday night."

"You don't have to."

"I know," she said. "I want to."

---
